title: “What do you think, prince? For that householder or householder’s son, do bodily or mental fevers arise due to craving? Burned by those fevers born…
content: “What do you think, prince? For that householder or householder’s son, do bodily or mental fevers arise due to craving? Burned by those fevers born of craving, does he experience suffering?” - “Yes, venerable sir.” - “That householder or householder’s son, prince, burned by fevers born of craving, experiences suffering. That craving has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, unable to arise in the future. Therefore I feel at ease.”

title: “Monks, thus I have opened the safe, secure path leading to happiness, closed the dangerous path, removed the male decoy, destroyed the female decoy. Monks,…
content: “Monks, thus I have opened the safe, secure path leading to happiness, closed the dangerous path, removed the male decoy, destroyed the female decoy. Monks, whatever a teacher should do for his disciples out of compassion, that I have done for you out of compassion. Monks, here are the roots of trees, here are empty places. Meditate, do not be heedless, do not have cause for regret later. This is my instruction to you.”

title: “One in whom there are no underlying tendencies, Roots of unwholesome states well pulled out — That monk abandons the near and far shore, Like…
content:
“One in whom there are no underlying tendencies,
Roots of unwholesome states well pulled out —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One in whom there is nothing born of anguish,
That might lead back to this shore —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One in whom there is nothing born of craving,
That might lead to continued existence —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One who has abandoned the five hindrances,
Free from anguish, free from uncertainty,
Gone beyond the dart —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

title: “Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What…
content: “Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of a skeleton, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse. These ten perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end.”

title: “And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification of sensual pleasures? Mahānāma, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye – desirable,…
content: “And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification of sensual pleasures? Mahānāma, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye – desirable, pleasurable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body – desirable, pleasurable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, Mahānāma, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure – that is the gratification of sensual pleasures.”

title: “Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and…
content:
“Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and humans delight in sound … in odor … in taste … in touch … in phenomena, are excited by phenomena. When phenomena change, fade, and cease, devas and humans dwell in suffering.

Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches,
And all phenomena —
Desirable, delightful, agreeable —
Thus they are called.

Devas and humans in the world,
Regarding them as delightful —
Where they cease and fade away,
Devas and humans see suffering.

The noble one sees as ease
When identity view is destroyed —
The noble one sees as opposite
All the views of the world.

What others call pleasure,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as pleasure.

See the Dhamma, hard to comprehend,
Where the ignorant are bewildered —
Darkness for the blind,
Obscurity for those who cannot see.

The wise are open-eyed,
Like light clearly shining,
The foolish, even though near,
Do not understand the Dhamma.

Overcome by the thirst of birth,
Swept away by the current of existence,
Subject to Māra’s control —
They do not awaken to this Dhamma.

Apart from the noble ones, no one
Awakens to this path —
The path leading to Nibbāna,
With perfect wisdom, free from defilements.”

title: Elder Nun Mother of Vaḍḍha: Vaḍḍha, never fall into the realm of sensual desire. My son, do not share In repeated suffering. Blissful is the…
content:
Elder Nun Mother of Vaḍḍha:

Vaḍḍha, never fall into the realm of sensual desire.
My son, do not share
In repeated suffering.

Blissful is the sage,
Without desire, with doubt cut off,
Cooled, self-controlled,
Without any defilements.

That sage practices
The path leading to right view,
Putting an end to suffering.
Vaḍḍha, strive on!

With confidence, mother spoke
This purpose for you —
“My dear mother! I think
That you have no sensual desire.”

“Vaḍḍha, whatever conduct —
Low, high, or middling —
Not even a little sensual desire
Exists in me.

I have destroyed all defilements,
Not heedless, meditating.
The three true knowledges are attained —
The Buddha’s instruction is done.”

Wonderful, my mother,
Encouraging and urging me,
With verses of truth,
Out of compassion.

Hearing my mother’s words,
Her motherly instruction,
I practiced the Dhamma gratefully,
Attaining security from bondage.

I am energetic, striving,
Day and night not lazy.
Well encouraged by my mother,
I attained the supreme purity.

title: “Monks, suppose there is urine mixed with various medicines. Then a person with jaundice comes, and someone says to him: ‘Good man, this urine is…
content: “Monks, suppose there is urine mixed with various medicines. Then a person with jaundice comes, and someone says to him: ‘Good man, this urine is mixed with various medicines. If you wish, drink it. While drinking, you will not delight in its color, smell, or taste. But after drinking, you will be at ease.’ That person might drink it after reflection, without refusal. While drinking, he does not delight in its color, smell, or taste. But after drinking, he is at ease. Monks, I say that this course of practice is like that simile — namely, a course of practice that is painful in the present but has pleasant results in the future.”

title: “Monks, there are these five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps badly; he wakes up…
content: “Monks, there are these five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps badly; he wakes up badly; he has bad dreams; devas do not protect him; impure things flow out, nocturnal emission. These, monks, are the five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. Monks, there are these five benefits for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps well; he wakes up well; he has no bad dreams; devas protect him; impure things do not flow out. These, monks, are the five benefits for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, and falls asleep.”

title: “And how, monks, does a monk dwell ‘as below, so above; as above, so below’? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this body from the soles…
content: “And how, monks, does a monk dwell ‘as below, so above; as above, so below’? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this body from the soles of the feet upward, from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin and full of various impurities: ‘There are in this body: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, intestinal mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, skin oil, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’ Thus, monks, a monk dwells ‘as below, so above; as above, so below.’”
